editor_overrides_about: Exact-text replacements the build applies to every string it takes from the makers' manifests and notes, the creative director's scores and the accessibility audit, so the editor can copy-edit those words on the board without editing another owner's file. Each entry is {"old": "exact text", "new": "replacement"}. The build warns for any "old" that matches nothing. The board's own words are edited in this file directly.
title: The stage B drawings, for your approval
deck: Every new or redrawn drawing from stage B sits on this board at true size, beside the drawing it replaces or the settled drawings, ones you have already approved, that it must stay apart from. Each new drawing comes in options so you can choose, as you asked on November 9 (DR-146). None of them enters the guide until you answer this board (DR-139).
facts: The board holds {n_cards} cards: the Civic Line drawings on cards 1 to {n_civic}, one choice for the whole utility set on card {family_n}, the utility icons on cards {first_action} to {last_action}, the pillar icons on card {pillars_n} and the identity drawings on cards {first_identity} to {n_cards}.

Each drawing shows at true size, the size a reader's screen will draw it, on Newsprint and in places on Charcoal too. Where the board draws one larger so you can see its pixels, a label says how many times larger.

The figures beside each option come from the creative director's scores and from the engineer's look-alike and pixel-fit checks, which run on the current files each time the board is built. It was last built on {built_date} at {built_time} UTC.
A number such as DR-146 points to one of your decisions in the decision log, and one such as D2-620 to a routine call the studio logged there.
ask: Look at each card's options at true size. The creative director's pick carries a Recommended mark and a one-line reason.
Choose one option on each card, or write your own answer in its note box. Every drawing here needs your approval by name (DR-139), so tick the card's "I approve by name" box when you agree.
Answer card {family_n} before the utility cards after it. It decides once, for the whole set, whether a utility icon stands bare or sits inside a ring.
Your marks collect in the reply panel at the end, one line per card, ready to paste into our chat.
sample_reply: All as recommended, and I approve every card by name.

legend.text: The creative director looked at each option with no label, at 48 px for a Civic Line drawing and 24 px for a utility icon, and wrote down what a first-time reader would most likely call it. Since the creative director knew the labels, the reading stands in for a first-time reader's. Real readers see some of these drawings, among them the pillar icons and the end mark, in the combined reader check after you answer (DR-143). A Civic Line verdict runs from Names the subject through Names it nearly, where the label settles it, and Recognized with the label to Misleads without the label. A utility icon's verdict is Names it, Names it nearly or Partly, where a reader names a near subject. The maker's verdict is the designer's own reading.

A look-alike figure says how alike two drawings look at 24 px on the engineer's check, on a scale from 0 to 1, where 1 means the same drawing. Among the 7,381 pairs of settled Civic Line drawings, one in 20 measures {watch} or more, and 74 pairs, one in 100, measure {flag} or more, most of them drawings built on a shared base, such as a page or a document with a different mark on it. The board flags a figure of {flag} or more, which asks for a look by eye, and marks one from {watch} up as one to watch. Before CL-014 B was redrawn, it measured 0.950 against R-46 Expand the House, and the creative director set the two side by side and found a reader will not take one for the other.

A pixel fit is a drawing redrawn for one small size so its lines land on whole pixels and its edges stay crisp. The engineer's pixel-fit check draws each file at 1x and at 2x. Its tests include lines at least one device pixel wide, straight edges on pixel edges, parts at least a pixel apart, no hole filling in and, where a drawing has a set line weight, a main line that matches it.

A device pixel is one dot of the screen. A 1x screen, such as many desktop monitors, gives each pixel of a drawing one device pixel. A 2x screen, the sharper kind on phones and many laptops, gives it two across and two down, so edges look smoother and a fit's pixels show as larger steps.

On November 8 you approved redrawing the domes and columns in six icons while keeping every other part and its red (DR-135). An option marked Within DR-135 does that. An option marked Outside DR-135 changes more, and its card says what.

The creative director scores each card from 1 to 5 on six criteria: craft, clarity, brand fidelity, usefulness, evidence honesty and accessibility. The score tables shorten brand fidelity to Brand and evidence honesty to Evidence. The guide's bar for shipping is 4 or more on every criterion, so the board boxes and names any score under 4 (D2-499).

civic.title: Civic Line drawings
intro: Six drawings lose a dome or columns (DR-135), and two new topic symbols join the set (DR-141). Each shows at 128, 48 and 24 px. Topic symbols are used from 48 px up, so the 24 px view is a reference size only (DR-136).

utility.title: The utility set
intro: Utility icons mark actions on a page, such as Close, Download and Search. They are one family on a 24-unit grid with a 2 px line, drawn in one color with no red, and each has its own 16 px drawing (DR-134). Each shows at 24 and 16 px, the two sizes the guide uses, on Newsprint and on Charcoal.

pillars.title: The pillar icons on whole pixels
intro: The pillar icons appear at 24 and 16 px, where on a 1x screen their master drawings' thin lines fall under one device pixel and blur. So each size gets a fit drawn on whole pixels (DR-133).

identity.title: Identity drawings
intro: The last three cards hold the end mark, the lockmark's small masters and L6. All three change identity geometry, which gate rule 4 says needs your approval by name.

congress.title: Congress: one sign for four drawings
lede: CL-025 Congress, CL-014 Entrenched Power, R-13 Congressional Capacity and R-42 Congressional Tariff Votes each lose their dome (DR-135). They share one Congress sign (D2-503). Each set draws that sign into {set_ids}, so you choose a set once, and each set's row sits under today's drawings.{own_line}
congress.honest: No set names Congress without its label. Most readers know Congress by the Capitol dome, which Rule 01.6 keeps out of icons, so the label names it, and the drawing's job is to make the label land at once (D2-620).
congress.neighbors_title: Beside the House drawings the guide keeps
congress.neighbors_text: {names} stay as drawn (DR-152). They sit here beside the chamber options so you can see the House drawings together.
congress.approve: One set, A, B or C, for {sets} together.
congress.own_line: {own} takes its own pick lower on this card, since the creative director recommends a different letter for it.
congress.follows: {ids} take the set you pick for {lead}.
congress.own_text: Choose one option for {id} here. The creative director's pick for it sits beside the set's pick in the recommendation below.
congress.approve_own: One set, A, B or C, for {sets} together, and one option for {own}.

redraw.pediment: Option A keeps its pediment as the record of what DR-135 approved. New options leave the pediment out with the rest of the classical front (D2-623).

lede: Testify is a new topic symbol for a member of the public speaking for the record at a public hearing, before a body such as a state legislative committee, a city council or a regulatory board (DR-141, the research lead's meaning sheet).
testify.neighbors_label: Settled drawings it must not be read as
testify.approve: One option for Testify, as a new topic symbol.

lede: Contact an official is a new topic symbol for a reader who calls, emails, writes to or visits the office of an official who represents them (DR-141, the research lead's meaning sheet). Option B is the simple phone you asked for, with an official at a desk at the cord's end so it reads as a call to an official's office (DR-147, DR-155).
contact.neighbors_label: Settled drawings it must not be read as
contact.approve: One option for Contact an official, as a new topic symbol.

utility-family.title: The utility family: bare actions or ringed
lede: On the look-alike check, actions drawn inside a ring measure as near twins of one another, so a row of them loses the outlines a reader tells apart. Each control on a page already has an outline of its own, so a ring repeats it. Error, Success and Warning keep a shape around them in both rows, since a bare check means selected and a bare exclamation mark is punctuation (D2-621). You decide the treatment once here, for every utility card after this one.
utility-family.approve: One treatment for the whole utility set.

rows.bare: Bare: each action's recommended option, with Error, Success and Warning in their shapes
rows.ringed: Ringed: every action in a ring, with the three marks still in their shapes

utility-family.unscored: The creative director answered this card as a family question and gave it no scores of its own. Each utility card's scores sit on that card.

utility.pair_approve: One pair for Play and Pause, picked together since one button swaps them (D2-557).
utility.lede: Used for: {label}. The accessibility audit asks for {asked}.
utility.pair_lede: {names} share one button, so you pick them as a pair (D2-557). The accessibility audit asks for {asked}.
utility.partners_title: If you pick the solid disc
utility.partners_text: With option {letter}, the check cut out of a solid disc, Error and Warning would take these solid partners, so the three marks stay one kind.
utility.own_asked: a drawing of its own and leaves the shape to the designer
utility.a11y_source: From the accessibility lead's check of the redrawn options (accessibility audit, section 9), in the lead's words.

pillars.title: The pillar icons at 24 and 16 px
lede: The Civic Line designer drew CL-019 Explain, CL-020 Track, CL-021 Connect and CL-022 Act pixel by pixel for 24 and 16 px. Every fit keeps every feature and every red placement of its master, with the red as its own shape (DR-133, D2-497). The black edition is the one in use under 48 px. At 24 px you choose between two line weights, and at 16 px one fit stands alone, since no second fit keeps every feature (D2-612).
pillars.approve: One 24 px fit for all four pillar icons, what 2x screens draw at 24 px, and the 16 px fit.
pillars.enlarged_label: Four times, to see the pixels
pillars.two_x: On a 2x screen a fit's pixels double into hard steps, and the master at 24 px draws smoothly with a line wider than one device pixel. A 24 px icon can therefore draw the fit on 1x screens and the master on 2x screens, and the engineer would build the switch by screen resolution (D2-634). At 16 px the master's line falls under one device pixel, so the fit serves both kinds of screen.
pillars.x2_caption: Each view is a 2x screen's render, shown {mag} times larger so you can see its pixels.

end-mark.title: The end mark on whole pixels at 14 and 12 px
lede: Ampersand B closes the last paragraph of an article as its end mark, at the height of the text's capitals (DR-130). These fits draw B on whole pixels for 17 px text (a 14 px B) and for 15 px text (a 12 px B), so its edges stay crisp on a 1x screen (DR-142). Fit A dips one pixel under the baseline, as today's end mark dips one or two, and Fit B sits on the baseline.
end-mark.stack_label: Today, Fit A and Fit B, one above the other at true size
end-mark.approve: One fit at 14 px and one at 12 px.
end-mark.illustrative: The paragraph is invented, to set the end mark in a line.
end-mark.two_x: On a 2x screen the fits double into 2 px steps, and today's end mark draws smoothly. The identity designer recommends the fit for 1x screens and today's end mark for 2x screens, and the engineer would build the switch by screen resolution (identity notes, question 2). Say so in the card's note if you want it otherwise.

lockmark.title: The lockmark's small masters rebuilt
lede: The identity designer rebuilt the 24 and 48 px lockmark masters with each node and the lever as one outline (DR-145). At their own sizes they draw today's pixels exactly. Between those sizes, where today's nodes part into light stripes, the rebuilt nodes stay whole. The 16 px master already draws each node as one circle, so it stays as it is (D2-542).
lockmark.approve: The rebuilt 24 and 48 px lockmark files.

l6.title: L6 with its wordmark and tagline centered
lede: L6, the strip that closes a report or a long page, shows here as drawn today without its dots (DR-129). Below it, the wordmark and tagline move down to sit on the strip's middle, as the lockmark does. That changes L6's proportion, so it needs your approval by name.
l6.approve: L6 with its wordmark and tagline centered.

reply.title: Ready to paste
text: Each line below is one card. Choose an option and tick "I approve by name" here or on the card itself; the two stay in step. Your answers collect in the box, ready to paste into our chat. Until you mark a card, the box holds the sample reply.
reply.storage: Your marks stay in this browser only.
